title: Scenario-driven routing playtest notes
summary: Working notes from a series of playtests exploring concrete routing decisions across regions and capacity tiers. Focus: pragmatic heuristics and micro decision-trees that balance latency, cost, and reliability for production LLM inference.
body:
Context:
- Objective: produce small, testable decision logic that ops/serving runtime can implement quickly. Avoid monolithic utility scoring for first pass; favor scenario-driven switch logic + lightweight fallback tree.
- Constraints: preserved latency SLOs for tier-A customers, aggressive cost controls for best-effort traffic, multi-region considerations (US/EU/APAC).

Core ideas:
1) Split decisions into two layers:
   - Fast-path selector (per-request, <1ms decision): cheap heuristics - client region, token budget, customer tier, route health flags.
   - Robust fallback tree (per-route state machine): invoked when fast-path signals risk (e.g., queueing, model OOMs, cross-region latency spike).

2) Use a compact decision tree representation that runtime can evaluate as a sequence of if/then rules. Avoid heavy ML scoring in control plane for now.

Example micro decision-tree (human-readable):

Start:
  if customer_tier == "enterprise" and route_local_capacity >= 1:
    route -> local-dedicated
  else if observed_p95_latency_local < latency_target and cost_score_local <= cost_threshold:
    route -> local-hosted
  else if region_health_remote == "degraded":
    route -> cheapest-available (with circuit breaker)
  else if token_budget > 1024 and remote_cost_saving >= 30% and p50_remote < latency_target + 30ms: 
    attempt -> remote-hosted (optimistic)
  else:
    route -> fallback-limited (truncate + cached-response)

Notes on signals used above:
- route_local_capacity: integer estimate of available slots in dedicated pool (fast heuristic).
- observed_p95_latency_local: short-window p95 from metrics stream (100–300ms window).
- cost_score_local: expected per-token cost for the candidate variant (including quantization).
- region_health_remote: boolean/enum from health-check aggregator (OK | degraded | offline).
- token_budget: request length + estimated completion length.

Policy heuristics and tradeoffs (practical observations from playtests):
- Latency-first for enterprise: prefer pinned dedicated pools; allow small cost overrun if it reduces p95 by >20ms.
- Cost-first for free/PLG: prefer hosted with quantized model variants; allow higher tail latency up to a soft cap.
- Reliability buffer: keep a reserved safety fraction (5–10%) of dedicated capacity for critical SLAs to avoid noisy neighbor loss during spikes.
- Cross-region optimistic routing: only enable when remote p50 is near local p50 and remote_region_health == OK; otherwise prefer local with best-effort fallbacks.

Fallback choreography examples:
- Model OOM on local-dedicated: immediate route to local-hosted-quantized; if that fails, route to remote-hosted with partial response flag and start async retry.
- Region short outage: short-circuit traffic to secondary region for enterprise routes; for PLG traffic, queue briefly (100–200ms) then attempt cheapest remote.

Decision-tree implementation notes (runtime-friendly):
- Represent tree as ordered rules with short-circuit returns. Keep <15 rules per route to keep eval fast.
- Use typed signals with expiry metadata (e.g., health flags expire after 10s).
- Provide a per-customer override map (small, hot cache) so CS/SE can pin customers to policies without redeploy.

Small example rule language (pseudo-DSL used in playtests):
RULES for customer_profile = "standard":
- if (local_capacity >= 2 and p95_local < 250ms) then SELECT local-hosted-q8h
- elif (tier == "enterprise" and local_capacity >=1) then SELECT local-dedicated
- elif (remote_p50 + 30ms < p95_local and remote_health == OK and remote_cost < local_cost * 0.7) then SELECT remote-hosted
- else SELECT fallback-cache

Observability and verification during rollout:
- Add explicit route labels in traces (route_decision = rule_id) so we can map errors/regressions back to specific rules.
- Create a small regression test harness that runs synthetic requests through the rule engine and asserts expected route choices under emulated signal sets.
- Metric counters: rule_evaluations_by_rule, decision_latencies, fallback_rates, cross_region_failover_count.

Playtest scenarios we ran (short notes):
- S1: sudden local GPU preemption (capacity drop to 0.3) -> enterprise traffic successfully moved to dedicated-hot standby via explicit rule; p95 increase +18ms; no customer-visible errors.
- S2: APAC inter-region link latency spike -> PLG traffic experienced 120ms added latency when optimistic remote routing was enabled; disabled remote-optimistic rule reduced cost by 12% at minor latency improvement.
- S3: hosted-quantized variant produced higher variance on long-context requests -> introduced token_budget guard to avoid sending long requests to quantized variants.

Open questions and next steps:
- How aggressive should optimistic remote routing be for mixed-tier customers? Need experiments with real traffic and feature-flagged cohorts.
- Should we encode backoff hysteresis in the rule engine (simple counters) or rely on health aggregator signals? Playtests suggest lightweight hysteresis reduces flip-flopping.
- Investigate compact binary format for rules to reduce control-plane wire cost for high-QPS routers.

Action items (owner notes):
- Diego: build regression harness to validate 10 canonical rule sets (due 2025-02-14).
- Marta: add trace instrumentation for rule_id and decision_latency (due 2025-02-07).
- Aisha: write draft runbook for operator overrides and safety caps (due 2025-02-21).

Appendix - simple ASCII decision tree sketch:
[Request] -> check customer_tier
   Enterprise? -> yes -> local_dedicated_available? -> yes -> local-dedicated
                                    -> no -> local-hosted-quantized if p95_ok else remote-dedicated-failover
   Enterprise? -> no -> p95_local_good? -> yes -> local-hosted
                                   -> no -> remote_candidate_ok? -> yes -> remote-hosted else fallback-cache

End of notes.

These are intentionally pragmatic, small, and observable-first rules intended to be incrementally deployed behind flags. The goal is to make the routing behavior debuggable and reversible while delivering clear latency and cost tradeoffs per customer tier.
